A pulley is suspended from the ceiling with a string OA. A block $\mathrm{m}_{2}\!=\!5\mathrm{kg}$ is connected via a thin rope passing over the pulley to another block $\mathrm{m}_{1}\!=\!2\mathrm{kg}$, which is suspended in the air. The inclined rope makes an angle $\alpha = 60^{\circ}$ with the vertical direction. The block $\mathbf{m}_{2}$ is at rest on the horizontal ground. The mass of the pulley and the rope, as well as the friction of the pulley, are negligible. The gravitational acceleration ${\bf g}$ is taken as $10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. Find the pressure of $\mathbf{m}_{2}$ on the ground and the magnitude of the frictional force acting on $\mathbf{m}_{2}$.
2. Determine the magnitude and direction of the tension force exerted by the string OA on the pulley.

40N, 10\sqrt{3}N
20\sqrt{3}N, direction is 30^{\circ} to the vertical, inclined to the upper left

Then reason: The masses and friction of the string and pulley are all neglected, so the tension is the same everywhere in the same string. m2 is stationary, and under the string-length constraint the system is stationary, so the suspended m1 is also in equilibrium. For m1: T = m1 g = 2 × 10 = 20 N. Force analysis on m2: the gravity m2g = 5 × 10 = 50 N is downward, the ground normal force N is upward, and the oblique-string tension T is along the string toward the upper left. The angle between the oblique string and the vertical direction is α = 60°, so the vertical component of the tension is T cos α, and the horizontal component is T sin α. Vertical equilibrium: N + T cos α = m2g, so N = 50 - 20 cos 60° = 50 - 10 = 40 N. The magnitude of the pressure of m2 on the ground is equal to the support force of the ground on m2, which is 40 N. Horizontal equilibrium requires the magnitude of static friction f = T sin α = 20 sin 60° = 10√3 N. Force analysis on the pulley: the string exerts two tensions on the pulley. One comes from the left vertical string, in the vertically downward direction, with magnitude T; the other comes from the right oblique string, in the direction along the oblique string toward the lower right, making an angle α with the vertical direction, with magnitude T. Therefore the resultant force components of the string on the pulley are: horizontally rightward T sin α, vertically downward T + T cos α. The pulling force of the suspension string OA on the pulley is opposite to this resultant force, so its components are horizontally leftward T sin α and vertically upward T + T cos α. Substituting T = 20 N and α = 60°: the horizontal component is 10√3 N, and the vertical component is 30 N. Its magnitude F = √[(10√3)^2 + 30^2] = √1200 = 20√3 N. raw_record.original_question:
A pulley is suspended from the ceiling with a string OA. A block $\mathrm{m}_{2}=5\mathrm{kg}$ is connected via a thin rope passing over the pulley to another block $\mathrm{m}_{1}=2\mathrm{kg}$, which is suspended in the air. The inclined rope makes an angle $\alpha=60^{\circ}$ with the vertical direction. The block $\mathbf{m}_{2}$ is at rest on the horizontal ground. The mass of the pulley and the rope, as well as the friction of the pulley, are negligible. The gravitational acceleration $\mathbf{g}$ is taken as $10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. Find the pressure of $\mathbf{m}_{2}$ on the ground and the magnitude of the frictional force acting on $\mathbf{m}_{2}$.
2. Determine the magnitude and direction of the tension force exerted by the string OA on the pulley.
raw_record.answer:
40N, 10\sqrt{3}N
20\sqrt{3}N, direction is 30^{\circ} to the vertical, inclined to the upper left
raw_record.final_cot:
First describe the image: In the figure, the pulley is suspended below the upper support point O, and a light string passes around the pulley; the left string segment goes vertically downward and connects to the suspended m1, and the right string segment goes obliquely downward to the right and connects to m2 placed on the horizontal ground. The dashed line in the figure is the vertical direction through the pulley, and the angle between the oblique string and the vertical direction is marked as α.

Then reason: The masses and friction of the string and pulley are all neglected, so the tension is the same everywhere in the same string. m2 is stationary, and under the string-length constraint the system is stationary, so the suspended m1 is also in equilibrium. For m1: T = m1 g = 2 × 10 = 20 N.

Force analysis on m2: the gravity m2g = 5 × 10 = 50 N is downward, the ground normal force N is upward, and the oblique-string tension T is along the string toward the upper left. The angle between the oblique string and the vertical direction is α = 60°, so the vertical component of the tension is T cos α, and the horizontal component is T sin α. Vertical equilibrium: N + T cos α = m2g, so N = 50 - 20 cos 60° = 50 - 10 = 40 N. The magnitude of the pressure of m2 on the ground is equal to the support force of the ground on m2, which is 40 N. Horizontal equilibrium requires the magnitude of static friction f = T sin α = 20 sin 60° = 10√3 N.

Force analysis on the pulley: the string exerts two tensions on the pulley. One comes from the left vertical string, in the vertically downward direction, with magnitude T; the other comes from the right oblique string, in the direction along the oblique string toward the lower right, making an angle α with the vertical direction, with magnitude T. Therefore the resultant force components of the string on the pulley are: horizontally rightward T sin α, vertically downward T + T cos α. The pulling force of the suspension string OA on the pulley is opposite to this resultant force, so its components are horizontally leftward T sin α and vertically upward T + T cos α. Substituting T = 20 N and α = 60°: the horizontal component is 10√3 N, and the vertical component is 30 N. Its magnitude F = √[(10√3)^2 + 30^2] = √1200 = 20√3 N. The angle θ with the vertical direction satisfies tan θ = (10√3)/30 = 1/√3, so θ = 30°, and the direction is toward the upper left.

First describe the image: In the figure, the pulley is suspended below the upper support point O, and a light string passes around the pulley; the left string segment goes vertically downward and connects to the suspended m1, and the right string segment goes obliquely downward to the right and connects to m2 placed on the horizontal ground. The dashed line in the figure is the vertical direction through the pulley, and the angle between the oblique string and the vertical direction is marked as α.

Then reason: The masses and friction of the string and pulley are all neglected, so the tension is the same everywhere in the same string. m2 is stationary, and under the string-length constraint the system is stationary, so the suspended m1 is also in equilibrium. For m1: T = m1 g = 2 × 10 = 20 N.

Force analysis on m2: the gravity m2g = 5 × 10 = 50 N is downward, the ground normal force N is upward, and the oblique-string tension T is along the string toward the upper left. The angle between the oblique string and the vertical direction is α = 60°, so the vertical component of the tension is T cos α, and the horizontal component is T sin α. Vertical equilibrium: N + T cos α = m2g, so N = 50 - 20 cos 60° = 50 - 10 = 40 N. The magnitude of the pressure of m2 on the ground is equal to the support force of the ground on m2, which is 40 N. Horizontal equilibrium requires the magnitude of static friction f = T sin α = 20 sin 60° = 10√3 N.

Force analysis on the pulley: the string exerts two tensions on the pulley. One comes from the left vertical string, in the vertically downward direction, with magnitude T; the other comes from the right oblique string, in the direction along the oblique string toward the lower right, making an angle α with the vertical direction, with magnitude T. Therefore the resultant force components of the string on the pulley are: horizontally rightward T sin α, vertically downward T + T cos α. The pulling force of the suspension string OA on the pulley is opposite to this resultant force, so its components are horizontally leftward T sin α and vertically upward T + T cos α. Substituting T = 20 N and α = 60°: the horizontal component is 10√3 N, and the vertical component is 30 N. Its magnitude F = √[(10√3)^2 + 30^2] = √1200 = 20√3 N.
